routes.description: Establish the motion through a cumulative case in which the universe's beginning requires a transcendent personal cause, objective moral values require a divine foundation, and the historical facts concerning Jesus are best explained by divine resurrection, while answering principal naturalistic objections.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cosmological, moral, and resurrection inferences jointly warrant a transcendent personal and moral foundation of reality, and if objections from naturalistic explanation, suffering, source reliability, and methodological limits do not defeat those inferences.

motionBridge.description: The supported cosmological, moral, and historical conclusions must jointly warrant that God exists as the transcendent personal cause and moral foundation of reality.

centralBridges.description: The universe must have begun to exist, and its beginning must require a transcendent, immaterial, personal cause rather than emergence from non-being.
Objective moral values and duties must be real and must require a transcendent divine foundation that evolutionary or social accounts do not supply.
The historical facts concerning Jesus must be established and divine resurrection must explain them better than the proposed natural alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The existence of suffering must remain compatible with God through the possibility of morally sufficient reasons for permitting it.
Philosophical reasoning must legitimately draw metaphysical consequences from scientifically informed premises without depending on an appeal to unexplained gaps.

routes.description: Defeat the motion by showing that no observed feature of reality requires God, that naturalistic accounts or open scientific inquiry remain available for cosmic origins, morality, and reported miracles, and that suffering conflicts with the proposed loving deity.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative inferences fail to establish their divine conclusions because their premises or explanatory bridges remain unsupported, natural alternatives remain viable, and the evidential challenge from suffering is not adequately reconciled with an all-loving God.

motionBridge.description: The motion fails if the universe, morality, and historical reports do not require a transcendent personal and moral foundation and the total evidence supplies no adequate basis for God.

centralBridges.description: Cosmic beginning, physical constants, and apparent order must admit naturalistic possibilities without requiring pre-universe causality, purpose, or a divine creator.
Moral conduct and distinctions must be explicable through biological and social development without requiring a divine source or judge.
The resurrection inference must lack sufficiently reliable historical evidence, with ordinary explanations remaining more credible than suspension of natural law.
Apparently gratuitous innocent suffering must count against the existence of the all-loving God specified by the affirmative position.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Claims about reality must be constrained by observation and testable theorizing rather than by metaphysical extrapolation or untestable divine intentions.
A divine entity must not be introduced when simpler explanations remain available in principle or scientific inquiry has not exhausted natural accounts.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Causality, and a Personal First Cause
sections.rationale: This issue contains the principal clash over whether the universe began, whether causality applies to that beginning, whether net-zero or successive-universe accounts alter the origin problem, and whether any required cause is personal and transcendent.

sections.title: Objective Morality and Its Foundation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether objective moral values and duties exist, whether evolutionary and social accounts explain only moral behavior or also binding validity, and whether a transcendent divine foundation is required by the motion.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Miracle Inference
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether the empty tomb, reported appearances, and origin of Christian belief are historically established, whether the sources are reliable, and whether divine resurrection is warranted over natural explanations.

sections.title: Suffering and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This issue matters because apparently gratuitous innocent suffering is offered as evidence against an all-loving God, while the opposing route requires showing that God could have morally sufficient reasons for permitting it.

sections.title: Scientific Explanation, Philosophy, and Divine Necessity
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether scientific evidence may support premises with theological consequences, whether metaphysical reasoning legitimately extends beyond empirical inquiry, and whether natural explanation makes God unnecessary without merely appealing to future discovery.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The universe began to exist, and its beginning therefore requires an uncaused, timeless, immaterial, transcendent personal cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Craig, and this uninterrupted opening argument precedes the handoff to Atkins.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the principal cosmological route and therefore has no earlier opposing move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central route with explicit premises and a stated conclusion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal syllogism and proposed attributes are recoverable, though the bridge from timeless cause to personhood is compressed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion follows if both premises hold, but the excerpt treats the personal-cause attributes more firmly than its compressed warrant supports.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The syllogistic core is valid, but the move leaves material bridges from a beginning to causation and especially personhood underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt supplies a structured inference but compresses the scientific support for a finite past and the warrant for personal agency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is indispensable direct support for the central cosmic-beginning bridge and sits at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily presents its own positive syllogism rather than interpreting a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly gives two premises, a necessary conclusion, and attributes the transcendent cause as uncaused, timeless, and immaterial.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Objective moral values and duties are binding independently of human belief, and their existence requires God as their transcendent foundation.
moves.attributionBasis: This is Craig's explicitly numbered second argument within his uninterrupted opening presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces the affirmative moral argument and has no earlier opposing locked move requiring an answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the conditional premise and defines the central concept of objective moral value.

precisionFindings.rationale: Objective validity is expressly defined, while the claim that only God can ground it remains an implicit exclusivity qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional is asserted categorically although the excerpt does not compare secular accounts of objective normativity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional structure is usable and consistent, but the exclusive bridge from objectivity to divine foundation is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The definition clarifies the explanandum, yet the crucial claim that objective duties require God is mainly asserted here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the affirmative route's indispensable moral-foundation premise and therefore ranks very high centrally.

representationalCharity.rationale: No developed opposing grounding theory is interpreted in this constructive excerpt, so meaningful charity is not tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig defines objective values as valid independently of belief and states that their existence depends on God, but the excerpt gives little rival comparison.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: The empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and origin of the disciples' resurrection belief are best explained by Jesus's divine resurrection, providing evidence that God exists.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig labels this his third argument and develops it continuously before summarizing his cumulative case.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the affirmative historical case and has no earlier opposing locked move to which it must respond.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies the claimed facts and explicitly connects their proposed explanation to God's existence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The three-fact inference is clear, though source independence and the meaning of majority recognition are left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Best-explanation language is probabilistic, but confidence exceeds the excerpt's documentation and comparison of natural alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive form is coherent, but the bridge from the three reports to divine resurrection requires a fuller rival comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific alleged historical facts are offered, but their establishment, independence, and superiority over alternatives remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the indispensable resurrection bridge by stating both the historical explananda and proposed divine explanation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt presents the affirmative explanation without developing a specific natural rival whose strongest form could be tested.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names the empty tomb and indicates three facts allegedly recognized by historians, then identifies resurrection as their best explanation.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: No observed feature of reality requires God because simpler explanations, or prospects for simpler explanations, remain available without adding the complex divine hypothesis.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the floor to Atkins, who states this as the governing thesis of his opening presentation.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the governing naturalistic-parsimony thesis and therefore has no earlier opposing locked move to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it establishes a relevant methodological thesis, but its universal scope is supported chiefly by prospect.

precisionFindings.rationale: The prospective qualification is explicit, but simpler explanation and absolutely everything remain materially broad and unstable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Adding prospects acknowledges incompleteness, yet the universal claim that everything has such a prospect substantially outruns the excerpt's support.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Availability of possible simpler explanations does not by itself establish that no divine explanation is needed, leaving a substantial modal bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The sweeping claim relies on an asserted prospect of future explanations and provides no representative support or comparison here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the explanatory-parsimony subsidiary bridge and is unusually broad within that supporting tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move advances a general naturalistic thesis without closely interpreting a particular opposing argument or qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Atkins expressly appeals to simpler explanations or their future prospect for absolutely everything, making the methodological scope and evidential limitation visible.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: An original universe need not have a prior cause because physical laws, including causal relations understood as summaries of observed behavior, arise with the universe itself.
moves.attributionBasis: Atkins identifies contingency as his first topic and develops the position continuously through his conclusion about a creator.

components.text: The beginning of the original universe requires a prior transcendent cause.
Causal principles legitimately apply beyond or prior to the universe.

response.rationale: Atkins diagnoses the prior-cause demand as naive because causal laws are summaries arising with the universe, and concludes that a prior creator is not required.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic replies, it explicitly attacks the decisive causal inference and states the consequence for a creator.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is clear, but treating all causality as a physical-law summary leaves the metaphysical scope partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The criticism strongly denies prior causation although the asserted account of causal relations does not exclude every metaphysical causal principle.

charity.alternative: Craig's causal premise is metaphysical rather than merely a physical law summarizing observations.
charity.decisiveQualification: The excerpt does not show that every metaphysical causal principle begins with physical law.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument coherently challenges temporal physical causation, but it needs a bridge from that point to rejection of metaphysical dependence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It offers a conceptual account of physical laws as summaries, but does not independently defend that account against the stronger premise.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the indispensable causal requirement in the affirmative cosmic-beginning bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply contacts the causal premise but narrows it to empirical physical-law causality without resolving the stronger metaphysical reading.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks whether an original universe had to be caused and answers by arguing that laws, including causal relations, arise with that universe.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: No reliable divine suspension of natural law has been established, and natural explanations are more credible than resurrection as an account of the reported events.
moves.attributionBasis: Atkins introduces miracles as his fourth topic and directly addresses resurrection claims raised earlier by Craig.

components.text: Divine resurrection reliably explains the reported historical events.
The specific empty-tomb, appearance, and belief reports are historically established.

response.rationale: The reply challenges reliable evidence for divine intervention, contacting the miraculous-explanation component but not examining the three alleged facts individually.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive miracle warrant while leaving the specific historical-fact case substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The thesis is recoverable, but observed and reliable evidence are not specified and the universal historical claim lacks qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim of not one atom of reliable evidence is much stronger than the representative support supplied in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: The resurrection case is a historical inference rather than a directly observed laboratory suspension of law.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical evidence could in principle warrant an event without contemporary direct observation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The skepticism is relevant, but absence of directly observed suspension does not by itself defeat a historical abductive claim.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The sweeping evidential denial is supported mainly by assertion and an institutional example rather than analysis of the cited reports.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the miracle warrant within the central resurrection bridge, though not every historical component.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply invokes reliability but largely substitutes nonobservation of law suspension for assessment of the historical inference actually offered.

moves.evidenceBasis: Atkins says miracles of suspended natural law have never been observed and denies reliable evidence of divine intervention, without treating each alleged fact.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: The torment, accident, and disease suffered by innocent people are more simply explained by the absence of an all-loving God and constitute evidence against such a deity.
moves.attributionBasis: Atkins introduces theodicy as a distinct fifth topic and completes the argument before turning to morality.

components.text: Objective moral values require God as their transcendent foundation.

response.rationale: The suffering argument bears on the motion but does not answer the earlier moral-grounding inference; no earlier locked affirmative suffering move was legally available.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it presents substantial contrary material but does not contact the selected earlier move's decisive demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential proposition is clear, although the restriction to apparently gratuitous innocent suffering is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Suffering is appropriately presented as evidence, but calling divine absence the simple explanation compresses comparison with possible theodicies.

charity.alternative: An all-loving God might permit suffering for morally sufficient reasons unavailable to limited observers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Mere logical possibility does not erase the evidential force of apparently gratuitous suffering.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidential inference is coherent, but the comparative premise that divine absence explains suffering better is compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete categories of innocent suffering support the explanandum, while prevalence, gratuity, and alternative comparison remain underdeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central suffering bridge by treating innocent suffering as evidence against an all-loving God.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move notes theologians' explanations only dismissively and does not assess their strongest form, though its evidential claim survives possibility alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies torment, accident, and disease affecting innocents and explicitly presents these phenomena as evidence against an all-loving deity.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: Moral distinctions emerged through evolutionary history and the human capacity to consider consequences, so morality does not require a divine source or judge.
moves.attributionBasis: Atkins labels morality his sixth and final point, and the delivered lookahead preserves the move through its concluding societal claim.

components.text: Moral distinctions require a divine source rather than natural development.
Evolutionary development explains objectively binding moral validity.

response.rationale: Atkins gives an evolutionary and consequence-sensitive origin for moral distinctions, but does not fully answer Craig's separate demand for mind-independent binding validity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the divine-source inference directly but leaves the objective-validity component unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The natural-origin proposition is recoverable, but morality shifts between behavior, distinctions, kindness, and binding standards.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The evolutionary account is presented as Atkins's view with some nuance, though its anti-foundational consequence is not fully warranted.

charity.alternative: Evolution may explain moral beliefs and behavior while leaving their objective validity unexplained.
charity.decisiveQualification: A genealogical explanation does not alone settle whether any moral proposition is objectively true.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The genealogy coherently explains capacities and conduct, but inferring no divine ground leaves a material is-to-ought and genealogy-to-validity gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Evolution and consequence-sensitive cognition provide a plausible sketch, but no specific evidence or warrant establishes normative sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central divine-grounding bridge, albeit by contacting only the natural-origin component.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses natural origins but does not preserve Craig's decisive distinction between the origin of belief and normative validity.

moves.evidenceBasis: Atkins attributes moral distinctions to evolutionary history and emerging consideration of consequences, directly offering a natural source account.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: God and evil are logically compatible if God could have morally sufficient reasons for permitting the evil found in the world.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs within Craig's announced rebuttal and directly addresses Atkins by name throughout the argument.

components.text: Innocent suffering is evidence against the existence of an all-loving God.
The absence of God explains suffering more simply than theism does.

response.rationale: Craig establishes possible logical compatibility through morally sufficient reasons, but that answer does not fully defeat Atkins's probabilistic evidential claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts compatibility but leaves the decisive comparative evidential force of suffering unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to logical consistency and expressly relies only on possible morally sufficient reasons.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest modal conclusion matches the offered possibility premise and is explicitly restricted to logical compatibility.

charity.alternative: Atkins advances suffering as probabilistic evidence, not necessarily as a strict logical contradiction.
charity.decisiveQualification: Logical compatibility alone does not remove evidential disconfirmation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: As a logical-compatibility argument the inference is explicit and valid, with only the possibility premise left substantively undefended.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The modal defense needs only possibility for compatibility, but no concrete account supports the proposed morally sufficient reasons.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the affirmative subsidiary compatibility bridge and ranks near the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig accurately states a logical defense but assigns Atkins an impossibility burden stronger than the evidential argument in the locked move.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly states that possible morally sufficient reasons establish consistency between God and evil, while shifting an impossibility burden to Atkins.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Nothing has no causal powers, and a zero balance of positive and negative energy neither makes existing reality nothing nor removes the need for a transcendent cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator has yielded the rebuttal to Craig, whose first-person argument explicitly names and critiques Professor Atkins.

components.text: An original universe need not have a prior transcendent cause.
Natural explanation removes the need to posit a divine cause.

response.rationale: Craig argues that a zero energy balance is still existing reality and cannot give nothing causal powers, thereby reasserting the need for a cause.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly contests the no-cause consequence, though it addresses a zero-energy version more than the causal-law diagnosis.

precisionFindings.rationale: The nothing-versus-zero-energy distinction is clear, while its applicability to Atkins's entire original-universe account is implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The critique strongly establishes that zero net energy is not nothing, but treats that correction as sufficient for a transcendent cause.

charity.alternative: Zero net energy concerns a balance within physical reality rather than the literal nonexistence of all entities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Correcting that category mistake does not independently prove a transcendent personal cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between nothing and balanced energy is coherent, but the further inference to a transcendent cause remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual rebuttal is specific, yet the quoted characterization of Atkins and the causal conclusion receive limited independent support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central natural-cosmos bridge by denying that zero-energy considerations dissolve the origin question.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies the strongest zero-energy reading reasonably well but overstates what defeating it establishes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes Atkins's positive-and-negative-energy balance claim and insists that the question of why the universe began still requires a cause.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: An infinite sequence of universes cannot be excluded by philosophical or theological examples concerning finite cosmic systems; whether there was a beginning must be decided by evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Atkins's rebuttal, and the passage responds explicitly to examples and claims attributed to Craig.

components.text: The universe or relevant cosmic sequence began to exist.
The origin question necessarily terminates in a transcendent cause.

response.rationale: Atkins directly contests exclusion of an infinite sequence and demands empirical evidence, thereby contacting the beginning premise and its causal consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly challenges the decisive finite-past premise, though it supplies little positive evidence for infinity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposal is explicitly framed as a sequence of universes that might be infinite and as an evidentially open question.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that infinity cannot be excluded and must be investigated by evidence matches the limited warrant offered.

charity.alternative: Philosophical arguments may bear on whether an actual infinite temporal sequence is coherent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Empirical evidence is not plainly the only relevant form of argument about possibility or infinity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand for evidence is consistent, but asserting that philosophy cannot bear on infinity is insufficiently supported and overly exclusive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply cites measured finite ages only to distinguish them from sequence length and offers no positive evidence for an infinite sequence.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable finite-beginning premise in the affirmative central cosmic bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Atkins fairly isolates the infinite-sequence issue but dismisses philosophical relevance too categorically rather than answering its strongest form.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes measured ages from the possible length of a universe sequence and explicitly says an infinite sequence must be assessed through evidence.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: The resurrection lacks the extraordinary evidence it requires because its Gospel reports are interested political constructions rather than sufficiently reliable historical records.
moves.attributionBasis: Atkins announces that he must address resurrection and miracles, then develops the skeptical historical argument in his own rebuttal.

components.text: The reported historical facts warrant divine resurrection as their best explanation.
The Gospel reports are sufficiently reliable and independent historical evidence.

response.rationale: Atkins directly raises the extraordinary-evidence threshold and attacks the Gospel reports as interested constructions, contacting evidence and inference components.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within full answers, it directly disputes the historical warrant and miracle threshold, though its source critique is thinly demonstrated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The skeptical conclusion is clear, but extraordinary evidence and political manifesto are rhetorically forceful terms without stable criteria.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion that the reports were invented as political construction substantially exceeds the source analysis shown in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Interested religious sources can still preserve historically useful testimony requiring source-by-source evaluation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Partisanship lowers confidence but does not by itself establish fabrication.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Demanding stronger evidence is coherent, but moving from extraordinary claim and interested sources to invention leaves a substantial bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The source-reliability conclusion relies heavily on assertion and political characterization rather than specific textual or historical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks both evidence reliability and explanatory sufficiency within the central resurrection bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the evidential issue but treats interested purpose as near-dispositive without handling the strongest qualified historical use.

moves.evidenceBasis: Atkins expressly says extraordinary evidence is absent and characterizes the Gospel material as politically interested rather than reliable historical documentation.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Evolution may explain contingent moral behavior or preferences, but it cannot ground objectively binding, mind-independent moral values and duties as a transcendent foundation can.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig explicitly labels the moral argument, corrects what he calls Atkins's misunderstanding, and restates both premises of his case.

components.text: Evolutionary origins make a divine source of morality unnecessary.
An account of moral behavior also grounds objective moral validity.

response.rationale: Craig diagnoses the genealogy as explaining contingent attitudes rather than objective validity and states that this leaves mind-independent duties ungrounded.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic replies, it explicitly identifies the genealogy-validity gap and gives its defeating consequence for the naturalistic account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evolved attitudes and mind-independent validity is explicit and consistently maintained throughout the excerpt.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The genealogical criticism is well fitted, but the further claim that only a transcendent foundation suffices remains compressed.

charity.alternative: Evolution can explain moral cognition while a secular realist theory separately grounds objective moral truths.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defeating evolutionary grounding alone does not exclude every secular account of validity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The origin-versus-validity distinction is logically strong, with the remaining gap located in the exclusive inference to transcendent foundation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The rewind scenario usefully illustrates contingency, but does not by itself establish objective truths or their uniquely divine ground.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central natural-morality bridge at its decisive claim to explanatory sufficiency.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig accurately targets Atkins's evolutionary account, but broadens its failure toward a divine-only conclusion without treating other secular realism.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts evolutionary spin-offs with objective validity and uses a rewind scenario to show that different moral attitudes could have evolved.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: When background evidence and comparative explanatory virtues are considered, divine resurrection is not intrinsically improbable and best explains the relevant historical facts.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig transitions to his third argument, names Atkins's Humean objection, and provides a structured two-part response before concluding his rebuttal.

components.text: The resurrection is too improbable to be warranted by the available evidence.
There is no reliable evidence of divine intervention in the reported events.
The Gospel reports are interested constructions rather than reliable records.

response.rationale: Craig contacts the improbability and comparative-explanation demands through a probability framework, but does not directly answer the political-source reliability attack.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive probability objection but leaves the separate source-reliability component substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparative probability claim is recoverable, although the relevant background evidence and explanatory virtues are only summarized.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Invoking background probability is appropriate, but the conclusion that resurrection best explains the facts exceeds the displayed comparison.

charity.alternative: The objection demands unusually strong evidence because ordinary natural explanations have much higher prior probability.
charity.decisiveQualification: Posterior probability depends on both prior probability and the comparative likelihood of the evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Bayesian-style correction is coherent, but the move compresses the likelihood comparison needed to establish resurrection as best.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It names the three alleged facts and a relevant probability framework, while documentation and serious comparison of rivals remain abbreviated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central naturalistic miracle-evidence bridge by addressing probability and explanatory comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: Craig identifies the strongest probabilistic structure of the objection and supplies the decisive background-evidence qualification, with limited numerical development.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig identifies a Humean improbability objection, invokes background evidence, and returns to the empty tomb, appearances, and origin of belief as explananda.

moves.speaker: Peter Atkins
moves.proposition: Untestable claims grounded in prior faith do not yield genuine explanation, whereas scientific inquiry advances cautiously through collected evidence toward understanding.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Atkins's second rebuttal, and Atkins immediately contrasts Craig's method with his own evidence-guided scientific approach.

components.text: Historical and background evidence can warrant the resurrection explanation.
Scientific evidence and philosophical inference warrant a transcendent cause.
Philosophical distinction rather than prior faith supports objective validity.

response.rationale: Atkins challenges the evidential status of Craig's resurrection reasoning as faith-led, but does not examine the specific evidence or probabilistic structure offered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers and weak partial replies, it contacts evidential method but not the decisive particulars of the arguments.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidence-versus-faith contrast is clear, but faith, demonstration, explanation, and science are drawn too broadly and dichotomously.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical portrayal of Craig as beginning only from faith is stronger than the excerpt's support and overlooks mixed evidential reasoning.

charity.alternative: Craig presents philosophical and historical arguments intended to use publicly assessable premises, not faith alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those arguments may still contain weak warrants without being reducible to prior faith.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Evidence-guided inquiry is a coherent norm, but the sharp faith-science dichotomy creates a false dilemma and does not defeat particular inferences.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological contrast is largely asserted, with no representative analysis showing that the earlier premises were produced solely by faith.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary evidential-method bridge, though its contact with the specific affirmative arguments is limited.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply materially weakens the opposing method by recasting its explicit arguments as mere starting faith rather than testing their warrants.

moves.evidenceBasis: Atkins contrasts cautious evidence collection with starting from belief in God and claims that faith-led explanation can accommodate anything.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.proposition: Scientific evidence may support the religiously neutral premise that the universe began, while philosophical argument draws its theological significance without appealing to a God of the gaps.
moves.attributionBasis: Craig answers the moderator's challenge in the informal discussion and carefully states the limited role he assigns scientific evidence.

components.text: Craig's theological conclusions arise from prior faith rather than evidence-guided inquiry.
Scientific inquiry alone makes metaphysical or divine explanation unnecessary.

response.rationale: Craig distinguishes a scientifically supported neutral premise from the later philosophical inference and explicitly denies using God to fill scientific gaps.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic replies, it identifies the alleged methodological conflation and states exactly how science and philosophy divide the work.

precisionFindings.rationale: The limited role assigned to science, the neutral premise, and the separate philosophical inference are all expressly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest methodological claim matches the excerpt: science is relevant to one premise and is not said to prove God directly.

charity.alternative: Scientific evidence may underdetermine whether the universe absolutely began and cannot itself establish a theological cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: Craig expressly limits science to supporting a neutral premise and assigns the further inference to philosophy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The division between scientific premise support and philosophical consequence is explicit, consistent, and answers the methodological conflation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual clarification is strong, though saying the beginning appears in any textbook is broad and the underlying science is not documented here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the evidential-method subsidiary bridge and is exceptionally focused within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the legitimate underdetermination concern while accurately restricting the scientific claim to its stated role.

moves.evidenceBasis: Craig calls the universe's beginning religiously neutral, says scientific evidence is relevant only to that premise, and denies a God-of-the-gaps appeal.
